metadata.title: Institutional characteristics moderating the relationship between classroom socioeconomic composition and teacher qualifications: Evidence from 46 education systems in TALIS 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher and school data collected under a two-stage stratified probability design (schools sampled with probability proportional to size; teachers randomly selected within schools). In the analysis, the authors state that “weights provided by TALIS for schools and teachers were included when possible,” and they also explicitly note that TALIS provides school weights used when aggregating school characteristics to the system (country) level. For the cross-school sorting robustness check, they report that “TALIS senate school weights” were applied, while for the main hierarchical models they describe using teacher/school weights where allowed by the estimation approach. For missing institutional variables, they create an imputed dataset (mice) and then run hierarchical models in Mplus; replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are not reported, and Mplus constraints are noted for including certain senate weights in 3-level Bayesian models.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses TALIS 2018 data for schools teaching ISCED 2 (lower secondary). The analytic sample is defined at the teacher/classroom level: the dependent variables are dichotomized teacher qualification statuses (novice = 5 or fewer years of experience; unspecialized = teachers who reported not studying a subject in formal education/training but reported currently teaching that subject). For robustness and subject-specific analyses, the authors restrict the sample to mathematics and science teachers (noted as narrowing to 48,725 mathematics and science teachers). For system-level (country) variables, they aggregate school-level measures to the country level using TALIS school weights and impute missing institutional variables using multivariate imputation by chained equations (mice), including country dummies and relevant school/teacher qualification variables in the imputation model.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 Lower secondary (ISCED 2) — teacher/classroom level (all subject domains)
main_findings.target_variable: Teacher with no specialization (math/science teaching mismatch)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Three-level random-slope model (Mplus) — coefficients and SEs reported in Table 3; no single aggregate ML metric (e.g., AUC/RMSE) reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 Lower secondary the study leveraged Classroom SES composition, Teacher gender, and classroom/school composition controls to model the odds of having a teacher with no specialization, finding that the classroom SES–specialization slope varies significantly across education systems and is moderated by system-level HDI (and other institutional factors show mixed/null patterns). This indicates that improving equitable access to subject-specialized teachers may require system-specific policy levers rather than one-size-fits-all reforms.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 Lower secondary (ISCED 2) — teacher/classroom level (all subject domains)
main_findings.target_variable: Teacher in the first 5 years of their career (novice teacher)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Three-level random-slope model (Mplus) — coefficients and SEs reported in Table 3; no single aggregate ML metric (e.g., AUC/RMSE) reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 Lower secondary the study leveraged Classroom SES composition and classroom/school controls to model the odds of having a novice teacher, finding that the classroom SES–novice slope varies significantly across education systems and that system-level school autonomy (staffing) and school competition are positively associated with the socioeconomic sorting slope in the novice models. This indicates that reducing novice-teacher inequities may depend on moderating marketization and decentralization in teacher staffing decisions, alongside targeted staffing supports for low-SES classrooms.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 (46 education systems; 9063 schools; 153,682 teachers) for lower secondary (ISCED 2), focusing on whether classroom socioeconomic composition predicts teacher qualification status. Teacher qualification is operationalized as novice (≤5 years experience) and unspecialized (no formal subject study but currently teaching the subject), with classroom SES measured via teacher perceptions of the share of socioeconomically disadvantaged students. The authors estimate within-country logistic regressions and then three-level random-slope generalized linear models in Mplus (classrooms/teachers nested in schools nested in education systems), using teacher/school weights where possible and imputing missing institutional variables via mice (mice package) with country dummies. Results are reported as odds ratios/coefficients with clustered SEs and show significant cross-system heterogeneity in the SES–qualification slopes, with system-level HDI relating more consistently to specialization sorting and system-level autonomy (staffing) and competition relating to novice sorting. Limitations include reliance on teacher-reported classroom SES and the absence of a single predictive ML performance metric (e.g., AUC/RMSE), as the models are regression-based rather than ML predictive modeling.
